description: A coder and innovator from UC Berkeley
summary: On a long space mission, a health reading matters only when an astronaut can understand what it means for them. CrewCompass brings daily check-ins and available health indicators into one clear dashboard. It helps each crew member compare changes with their own baseline, spot patterns that may need attention, and choose a next step—such as recording symptoms or contacting the medical team. NASA spaceflight health research informs which indicators the tool highlights. By turning scattered readings into understandable trends, CrewCompass supports earlier awareness and better-informed decisions when medical care is far from Earth.
details:
CrewCompass is a browser-based health monitoring prototype for long-duration space missions. It brings together two kinds of information: a real ISS radiation-environment sample from NASA’s OSDR RadLab and a crew member’s self-reported check-in, such as sleep and energy. The dashboard presents readings and trends in a clear format, helping crew members add personal context and decide when to note a symptom or follow mission medical procedures.

The goal is to make health information easier to understand and act on when a crew member is far from Earth and needs to monitor changes themselves. CrewCompass is creative in keeping environmental sensor readings separate from personal check-ins, while showing how both can inform a follow-up. The prototype uses sample check-in inputs; it is not a diagnostic tool and does not claim that radiation readings measure an astronaut’s individual exposure or health.

I developed an interactive web prototype using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with no custom hardware. We considered readability, individual baselines, limited medical support during missions, privacy, and the limits of interpreting sensor data in isolation.
